claim: Meningeal lymphatic vessels exist in humans.
source: Here, we report the existence of meningeal lymphatic vessels in human and nonhuman primates (common marmoset monkeys)
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical data showing lymphatic endothelial markers in human dura mater samples (Figures 3, 4) and MRI visualization in 5/5 human volunteers (Figure 1).

claim: Meningeal lymphatic vessels exist in nonhuman primates (common marmoset monkeys).
source: Here, we report the existence of meningeal lymphatic vessels in human and nonhuman primates (common marmoset monkeys)
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical data showing lymphatic endothelial markers in marmoset dura mater samples (Figure 4) and MRI visualization in 3/3 marmosets (Figure 1).

claim: Meningeal lymphatic vessels can be visualized noninvasively in vivo with high-resolution clinical MRI.
source: Here, we report the existence of meningeal lymphatic vessels in human and nonhuman primates (common marmoset monkeys) and the feasibility of noninvasively imaging and mapping them in vivo with high-resolution, clinical MRI.
evidence: Demonstrated by successful MRI visualization in 5/5 humans and 3/3 marmosets using T2-FLAIR and T1-weighted black-blood imaging after gadobutrol injection.

claim: Meningeal lymphatic vessels enhance with gadobutrol on T2-FLAIR imaging.
source: On T2-FLAIR and T1-weighted black-blood imaging, lymphatic vessels enhance with gadobutrol, a gadolinium-based contrast agent with high propensity to extravasate across a permeable capillary endothelial barrier
evidence: Shown by MRI images in Figure 1 and Figure 2 demonstrating enhancement of lymphatic vessels after gadobutrol administration.

claim: Meningeal lymphatic vessels enhance with gadobutrol on T1-weighted black-blood imaging.
source: On T2-FLAIR and T1-weighted black-blood imaging, lymphatic vessels enhance with gadobutrol, a gadolinium-based contrast agent with high propensity to extravasate across a permeable capillary endothelial barrier
evidence: Shown by MRI images in Figure 2 demonstrating enhancement of lymphatic vessels after gadobutrol administration.

claim: Meningeal lymphatic vessels do not enhance with gadofosveset.
source: On T2-FLAIR and T1-weighted black-blood imaging, lymphatic vessels enhance with gadobutrol, a gadolinium-based contrast agent with high propensity to extravasate across a permeable capillary endothelial barrier, but not with gadofosveset, a blood-pool contrast agent.
evidence: Demonstrated by MRI images in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing lack of lymphatic vessel enhancement after gadofosveset administration.

claim: Gadobutrol is a gadolinium-based contrast agent with high propensity to extravasate across a permeable capillary endothelial barrier.
source: On T2-FLAIR and T1-weighted black-blood imaging, lymphatic vessels enhance with gadobutrol, a gadolinium-based contrast agent with high propensity to extravasate across a permeable capillary endothelial barrier
evidence: This is established knowledge about gadobutrol's pharmacological properties and is supported by the differential enhancement patterns observed in the study.

claim: Gadofosveset is a blood-pool contrast agent.
source: On T2-FLAIR and T1-weighted black-blood imaging, lymphatic vessels enhance with gadobutrol, a gadolinium-based contrast agent with high propensity to extravasate across a permeable capillary endothelial barrier, but not with gadofosveset, a blood-pool contrast agent.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gadofosveset's pharmacological properties, confirmed by citation (Lauffer et al., 1998) and demonstrated by its intravascular retention in the study.

claim: The topography of meningeal lymphatic vessels in primates runs alongside dural venous sinuses.
source: The topography of these vessels, running alongside dural venous sinuses, recapitulates the meningeal lymphatic system of rodents.
evidence: Demonstrated by MRI images (Figures 1, 2, Videos 1-2) and histopathology (Figures 3, 4) showing lymphatic vessels parallel to venous sinuses.

claim: The topography of meningeal lymphatic vessels in primates recapitulates the meningeal lymphatic system of rodents.
source: The topography of these vessels, running alongside dural venous sinuses, recapitulates the meningeal lymphatic system of rodents.
evidence: Based on comparison with previously published rodent studies (Aspelund et al., 2015; Louveau et al., 2015b) and the observed anatomical distribution in primates.

claim: Meningeal lymphatics in primates display a typical panel of lymphatic endothelial markers by immunohistochemistry.
source: In primates, meningeal lymphatics display a typical panel of lymphatic endothelial markers by immunohistochemistry.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemical staining showing LYVE-1, D2-40 podoplanin, PROX1, COUP-TFII, and CCL21 expression in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: A network of true lymphatic vessels exists within the mammalian dura mater.
source: Recent reports (Aspelund et al., 2015; Louveau et al., 2015b) described the existence of a network of true lymphatic vessels within the mammalian dura mater that runs alongside blood vessels, notably the superior sagittal and transverse sinuses.
evidence: Based on cited studies in rodents (Aspelund et al., 2015; Louveau et al., 2015b).

claim: Dural lymphatic vessels run alongside blood vessels, notably the superior sagittal and transverse sinuses.
source: Recent reports (Aspelund et al., 2015; Louveau et al., 2015b) described the existence of a network of true lymphatic vessels within the mammalian dura mater that runs alongside blood vessels, notably the superior sagittal and transverse sinuses.
evidence: Based on cited studies (Aspelund et al., 2015; Louveau et al., 2015b) and confirmed by current study's MRI and histopathology data.

claim: Dural lymphatic vessels display typical immunohistochemical markers that identify lymphatic vessels elsewhere in the body.
source: The dural lymphatic vessels display typical immunohistochemical markers that identify lymphatic vessels elsewhere in the body.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemical staining in Figures 3 and 4, with positive controls from human skin shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dural lymphatic vessels provide an alternate conduit for drainage of immune cells from the brain.
source: They provide an alternate conduit for drainage of immune cells and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the brain, beyond previously described pathways of flow: via arachnoid granulations into the dural venous sinuses, and via the cribriform plate into the ethmoid region (Weller et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on cited reference (Weller et al., 2009) and inference from the anatomical location and lymphatic nature of the vessels.

claim: Dural lymphatic vessels provide an alternate conduit for drainage of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the brain.
source: They provide an alternate conduit for drainage of immune cells and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the brain, beyond previously described pathways of flow: via arachnoid granulations into the dural venous sinuses, and via the cribriform plate into the ethmoid region (Weller et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on cited reference (Weller et al., 2009) and inference from the anatomical location and lymphatic nature of the vessels.

claim: Previously described pathways of CSF drainage include flow via arachnoid granulations into the dural venous sinuses.
source: They provide an alternate conduit for drainage of immune cells and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the brain, beyond previously described pathways of flow: via arachnoid granulations into the dural venous sinuses, and via the cribriform plate into the ethmoid region (Weller et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on cited reference (Weller et al., 2009) describing established CSF drainage pathways.

claim: Previously described pathways of CSF drainage include flow via the cribriform plate into the ethmoid region.
source: They provide an alternate conduit for drainage of immune cells and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the brain, beyond previously described pathways of flow: via arachnoid granulations into the dural venous sinuses, and via the cribriform plate into the ethmoid region (Weller et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on cited reference (Weller et al., 2009) describing established CSF drainage pathways.

claim: Early reports based on India ink injections suggested that the dural pathway accounts for only a minority of CSF drainage.
source: Although early reports, based on injections of India ink into the cisterna magna of the rat, suggested that the dural pathway accounts for only a minority of the drainage (Kida et al., 1993)
evidence: Based on cited reference (Kida et al., 1993) describing earlier experimental findings.

claim: More recent studies indicate that the dural lymphatic system may be substantially more important for drainage of macromolecules and immune cells than previously realized.
source: the more recent studies (Aspelund et al., 2015; Louveau et al., 2015b), which are based on injections of fluorescent tracers and in vivo microscopy, indicate that the dural system may be substantially more important for drainage of macromolecules and immune cells than previously realized.
evidence: Based on cited references (Aspelund et al., 2015; Louveau et al., 2015b) describing more recent experimental findings.

claim: Whether a similar network of dural lymphatics is present in primates was previously unknown.
source: Whether a similar network of dural lymphatics is present in primates remains unknown.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

claim: Noninvasive visualization of dural lymphatics had not been reported prior to this study.
source: Moreover, noninvasive visualization of the dural lymphatics – a necessary first step to understanding their normal physiology and potential aberrations in neurological diseases – has not been reported.
evidence: This statement establishes the novelty of the current study's approach.

claim: The existence of a dural lymphatic network in humans was verified pathologically.
source: We therefore verified pathologically the existence of a dural lymphatic network in human and nonhuman primates (common marmoset monkeys)
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemical analysis of human dura mater samples shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The existence of a dural lymphatic network in nonhuman primates (common marmoset monkeys) was verified pathologically.
source: We therefore verified pathologically the existence of a dural lymphatic network in human and nonhuman primates (common marmoset monkeys)
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemical analysis of marmoset dura mater samples shown in Figure 4.

claim: T2-FLAIR is the clinical standard for detecting lesions within the brain parenchyma.
source: First, the T2-weighted fluid-attenuation inversion recovery (T2-FLAIR) pulse sequence, which is the clinical standard for detecting lesions within the brain parenchyma
evidence: This is established knowledge about clinical MRI practice.

claim: T2-FLAIR is highly sensitive to the presence of gadolinium-based contrast agents in the CSF.
source: First, the T2-weighted fluid-attenuation inversion recovery (T2-FLAIR) pulse sequence, which is the clinical standard for detecting lesions within the brain parenchyma, is highly sensitive to the presence of gadolinium-based contrast agents in the CSF (Mamourian et al., 2000; Mathews et al., 1999; Absinta et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on cited references (Mamourian et al., 2000; Mathews et al., 1999; Absinta et al., 2015) describing T2-FLAIR properties.

claim: Black-blood imaging sequences are typically used for measurement of vascular wall thickness or detection of atherosclerotic plaque.
source: Second, 'black-blood' imaging sequences, which are typically used for measurement of vascular wall thickness or detection of atherosclerotic plaque
evidence: This is established knowledge about clinical MRI applications.

claim: Black-blood imaging sequences are tuned to darken the contents of blood vessels even when they contain gadolinium-based contrast agent.
source: Second, 'black-blood' imaging sequences, which are typically used for measurement of vascular wall thickness or detection of atherosclerotic plaque, are tuned to darken the contents of blood vessels (even when they contain a gadolinium-based contrast agent)
evidence: This is established knowledge about black-blood imaging technique properties.

claim: Black-blood imaging may highlight vessels with contents and flow properties different from blood vessels.
source: Second, 'black-blood' imaging sequences, which are typically used for measurement of vascular wall thickness or detection of atherosclerotic plaque, are tuned to darken the contents of blood vessels (even when they contain a gadolinium-based contrast agent), but in the process the images may highlight vessels with other contents and flow properties (Mandell et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on cited reference (Mandell et al., 2017) and demonstrated by the current study's results.

claim: Postcontrast T1-weighted MPRAGE depicts avid enhancement of dura mater and blood vessels.
source: For comparison, we also acquired a postcontrast T1-weighted Magnetization Prepared Rapid Acquisition of Gradient Echoes (MPRAGE) MRI sequence, which is widely implemented for structural brain imaging and depicts avid enhancement of dura mater and blood vessels
evidence: This is established knowledge about T1-weighted MPRAGE properties, confirmed by images in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: T1-weighted MPRAGE would not be expected to discriminate lymphatic vessels.
source: For comparison, we also acquired a postcontrast T1-weighted Magnetization Prepared Rapid Acquisition of Gradient Echoes (MPRAGE) MRI sequence, which is widely implemented for structural brain imaging and depicts avid enhancement of dura mater and blood vessels, but which would not be expected to discriminate lymphatic vessels.
evidence: This is a prediction based on known properties of T1-weighted MPRAGE, confirmed by the study's results shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Cerebral blood vessels have a highly regulated blood-brain barrier.
source: Cerebral blood vessels have a highly regulated blood-brain barrier, protecting the neuropil from many contents of the circulating blood.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebrovascular physiology.

claim: The blood-brain barrier protects the neuropil from many contents of the circulating blood.
source: Cerebral blood vessels have a highly regulated blood-brain barrier, protecting the neuropil from many contents of the circulating blood.
evidence: This is established knowledge about blood-brain barrier function.

claim: Under physiological conditions, the blood-brain barrier prevents gadolinium-based chelates from passing into the Virchow-Robin perivascular spaces.
source: Under physiological conditions, the blood-brain barrier prevents gadolinium-based chelates in standard clinical use from passing into the Virchow-Robin perivascular spaces and parenchyma, so that these structures do not enhance on MRI.
evidence: This is established knowledge about blood-brain barrier properties and gadolinium contrast behavior.

claim: Under physiological conditions, the blood-brain barrier prevents gadolinium-based chelates from passing into the brain parenchyma.
source: Under physiological conditions, the blood-brain barrier prevents gadolinium-based chelates in standard clinical use from passing into the Virchow-Robin perivascular spaces and parenchyma, so that these structures do not enhance on MRI.
evidence: This is established knowledge about blood-brain barrier properties and gadolinium contrast behavior.

claim: Dural blood vessels lack a blood-meningeal barrier.
source: On the other hand, dural blood vessels lack a blood-meningeal barrier, enabling leakage of circulating fluids and small substances, including gadolinium-based compounds.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dural vascular physiology.

claim: Dural blood vessels enable leakage of circulating fluids and small substances, including gadolinium-based compounds.
source: On the other hand, dural blood vessels lack a blood-meningeal barrier, enabling leakage of circulating fluids and small substances, including gadolinium-based compounds.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dural vascular physiology, confirmed by the observed dural enhancement patterns.

claim: Thin dural enhancement is seen on conventional T1-weighted MRI scans under physiological conditions.
source: This explains the thin, though often incomplete, dural enhancement that is seen on conventional T1-weighted MRI scans under physiological conditions (Figure 1)
evidence: Demonstrated by MRI images in Figure 1 and based on established clinical MRI knowledge.

claim: Dural enhancement can show abnormal diffuse or localized thickening in a variety of pathological conditions.
source: This explains the thin, though often incomplete, dural enhancement that is seen on conventional T1-weighted MRI scans under physiological conditions (Figure 1), as well as its abnormal diffuse or localized thickening in a variety of pathological conditions (Smirniotopoulos et al., 2007; Antony et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on cited references (Smirniotopoulos et al., 2007; Antony et al., 2015) describing pathological dural enhancement patterns.

claim: Dural lymphatic vessels were visualized in 5/5 human healthy volunteers using high-resolution T2-FLAIR and T1-weighted black-blood MRI after gadobutrol injection.
source: Using high-resolution (in-plane resolution 270 × 270 μm or finer) T2-FLAIR and T1-weighted black-blood MRI images, obtained after the intravenous injection of standard FDA-approved contrast material (gadobutrol), we were able to visualize the collection of interstitial gadolinium within dural lymphatic vessels (maximum apparent diameter ~1 mm) in 5/5 human healthy volunteers and 3/3 common marmoset monkeys (Figure 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by MRI data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Dural lymphatic vessels were visualized in 3/3 common marmoset monkeys using high-resolution T2-FLAIR and T1-weighted black-blood MRI after gadobutrol injection.
source: Using high-resolution (in-plane resolution 270 × 270 μm or finer) T2-FLAIR and T1-weighted black-blood MRI images, obtained after the intravenous injection of standard FDA-approved contrast material (gadobutrol), we were able to visualize the collection of interstitial gadolinium within dural lymphatic vessels (maximum apparent diameter ~1 mm) in 5/5 human healthy volunteers and 3/3 common marmoset monkeys (Figure 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by MRI data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The maximum apparent diameter of dural lymphatic vessels visualized by MRI is approximately 1 mm.
source: Using high-resolution (in-plane resolution 270 × 270 μm or finer) T2-FLAIR and T1-weighted black-blood MRI images, obtained after the intravenous injection of standard FDA-approved contrast material (gadobutrol), we were able to visualize the collection of interstitial gadolinium within dural lymphatic vessels (maximum apparent diameter ~1 mm) in 5/5 human healthy volunteers and 3/3 common marmoset monkeys (Figure 1).
evidence: Based on measurements from MRI images.

claim: In the dura, small intravascular molecules extravasate into the interstitium and collect into lymphatic capillaries through a loose lymphatic endothelium under a hydrostatic pressure gradient.
source: Our results suggest that in the dura, similar to many other organs throughout the body, small intravascular molecules extravasate into the interstitium and then, under a hydrostatic pressure gradient, collect into lymphatic capillaries through a loose lymphatic endothelium (Sharma et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's MRI findings and cited reference (Sharma et al., 2008) describing general lymphatic physiology.

claim: Gadofosveset binds reversibly to serum albumin.
source: Gadofosveset binds reversibly to serum albumin, increasing its molecular weight from 0.9 to 67 kDa.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gadofosveset's pharmacological properties, supported by citation (Lauffer et al., 1998).

claim: Gadofosveset binding to serum albumin increases its molecular weight from 0.9 to 67 kDa.
source: Gadofosveset binds reversibly to serum albumin, increasing its molecular weight from 0.9 to 67 kDa.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gadofosveset's pharmacological properties.

claim: Under physiological conditions, albumin has a low transcapillary exchange rate into the interstitial compartment, estimated to be on the order of 5% per hour.
source: Under physiological conditions, albumin has a low transcapillary exchange rate into the interstitial compartment, estimated to be on the order of 5% per hour, which explains the propensity of gadofosveset to remain within blood vessels (Richardson et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on cited reference (Richardson et al., 2015) describing albumin physiology.

claim: The low transcapillary exchange rate of albumin explains the propensity of gadofosveset to remain within blood vessels.
source: Under physiological conditions, albumin has a low transcapillary exchange rate into the interstitial compartment, estimated to be on the order of 5% per hour, which explains the propensity of gadofosveset to remain within blood vessels (Richardson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on albumin physiology cited from Richardson et al., 2015, confirmed by the study's MRI findings.

claim: Gadofosveset did not reveal dural lymphatics in both human and nonhuman primates, especially on T1-black blood images.
source: In both species, gadofosveset did not reveal dural lymphatics, especially on T1-black blood images (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by MRI images in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gadofosveset provided superior intravascular enhancement in both meningeal and parenchymal blood vessels compared to gadobutrol on T1-weighted MPRAGE images.
source: As expected, on T1-weighted MPRAGE images, gadofosveset provided superior intravascular enhancement, in both meningeal and parenchymal blood vessels, compared to gadobutrol (Figure 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by MRI images in Figure 2.

claim: Dural lymphatics are localized around dural sinuses, middle meningeal artery, and cribriform plate.
source: Dural lymphatics (red arrows in magnified view boxes) were better discerned using gadobutrol (standard MRI contrast agent, which readily enters the dura) compared to gadofosveset (serum albumin-binding contrast agent, which remains largely intravascular) and were localized around dural sinuses, middle meningeal artery, and cribriform plate (white arrows).
evidence: Demonstrated by MRI images in Figure 2 and anatomical renderings in Videos 1-2.

claim: Dural lymphatics run parallel to the dural venous sinuses, especially the superior sagittal and straight sinuses.
source: On 3D-rendering of subtraction MRI images (Videos 1–2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), dural lymphatics are seen running parallel to the dural venous sinuses, especially the superior sagittal and straight sinuses, and alongside branches of the middle meningeal artery.
evidence: Demonstrated by 3D renderings in Videos 1-2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dural lymphatics run alongside branches of the middle meningeal artery.
source: On 3D-rendering of subtraction MRI images (Videos 1–2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), dural lymphatics are seen running parallel to the dural venous sinuses, especially the superior sagittal and straight sinuses, and alongside branches of the middle meningeal artery.
evidence: Demonstrated by 3D renderings in Videos 1-2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The topography of meningeal lymphatics visualized by MRI fits with the previously described network in rodents.
source: The topography of the meningeal lymphatics fits with the previously described network in rodents as well as our neuropathological data (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: Based on comparison with rodent studies (Aspelund et al., 2015; Louveau et al., 2015b) and confirmed by histopathology in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The lymphatics visualized by MRI are large slow-flow lymphatic ducts.
source: It is worth noting that the lymphatics visualized by MRI are large slow-flow lymphatic ducts, whereas blind-ending and small lymphatic capillaries, clearly seen by histopathology (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), are unlikely to be revealed by MRI.
evidence: This is an inference based on the resolution limits of MRI and comparison with histopathology.

claim: Blind-ending and small lymphatic capillaries are clearly seen by histopathology.
source: It is worth noting that the lymphatics visualized by MRI are large slow-flow lymphatic ducts, whereas blind-ending and small lymphatic capillaries, clearly seen by histopathology (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), are unlikely to be revealed by MRI.
evidence: Demonstrated by histopathological images in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Small lymphatic capillaries are unlikely to be revealed by MRI.
source: It is worth noting that the lymphatics visualized by MRI are large slow-flow lymphatic ducts, whereas blind-ending and small lymphatic capillaries, clearly seen by histopathology (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), are unlikely to be revealed by MRI.
evidence: This is an inference based on the resolution limits of MRI compared to histopathology.

claim: The induction of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) did not affect detection of dural lymphatic vessels in the two marmosets tested.
source: The induction of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) did not affect detection of dural lymphatic vessel in either of the two animals that we tested (not shown).
evidence: Based on experimental observations in two EAE marmosets.

claim: Within the dura mater, lymphatic and blood vessels can be differentiated using double immunostaining for PROX1 and CD31.
source: (D, F, G) Within the dura mater, lymphatic and blood vessels can be differentiated using double immunostaining for PROX1 (a transcription factor involved in lymphangiogenesis, nuclear staining) and CD31 (a vascular endothelial cell marker).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemical images in Figure 3.

claim: PROX1 is a transcription factor involved in lymphangiogenesis.
source: (D, F, G) Within the dura mater, lymphatic and blood vessels can be differentiated using double immunostaining for PROX1 (a transcription factor involved in lymphangiogenesis, nuclear staining) and CD31 (a vascular endothelial cell marker).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PROX1 function.

claim: CD31 is a vascular endothelial cell marker.
source: (D, F, G) Within the dura mater, lymphatic and blood vessels can be differentiated using double immunostaining for PROX1 (a transcription factor involved in lymphangiogenesis, nuclear staining) and CD31 (a vascular endothelial cell marker).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CD31 function.

claim: Lymphatic and blood vessels can be differentiated using double staining for podoplanin (D2-40) and CD31.
source: (E, H–K) Similarly, lymphatic and blood vessels can be differentiated using immunohistochemical (E, H, I) and immunofluorescent (J, K) double staining for podoplanin (D2-40, endothelial membrane staining) and CD31.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemical and immunofluorescent images in Figure 3.

claim: Red blood cells are seen within blood vessels, but not within lymphatic vessels.
source: Red blood cells are seen within blood vessels, but not within lymphatic vessels.
evidence: Demonstrated by histopathological images in Figure 3.

claim: Three clusters of cells surrounding the superior sagittal sinus and positive for lymphatic endothelial cell markers correspond to three enhancing areas seen on MRI.
source: (C-F) Three clusters of cells (circles), surrounding the SSS and positive for lymphatic endothelial cell markers, correspond to the three enhancing areas seen on MRI (A).
evidence: Demonstrated by direct MRI-histopathology correlation in Figure 4.

claim: LYVE-1 is a lymphatic endothelial cell marker with membrane staining.
source: LYVE-1 is a lymphatic endothelial cell marker (membrane staining), PROX1 and COUP-TFII are transcription factors involved in lymphangiogenesis (nuclear staining), and CCL21 is a chemokine implicated in lymphatic transmigration.
evidence: This is established knowledge about LYVE-1 function, confirmed by staining patterns in Figure 4.

claim: PROX1 and COUP-TFII are transcription factors involved in lymphangiogenesis with nuclear staining.
source: LYVE-1 is a lymphatic endothelial cell marker (membrane staining), PROX1 and COUP-TFII are transcription factors involved in lymphangiogenesis (nuclear staining), and CCL21 is a chemokine implicated in lymphatic transmigration.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PROX1 and COUP-TFII function, confirmed by staining patterns in Figure 4.

claim: CCL21 is a chemokine implicated in lymphatic transmigration.
source: LYVE-1 is a lymphatic endothelial cell marker (membrane staining), PROX1 and COUP-TFII are transcription factors involved in lymphangiogenesis (nuclear staining), and CCL21 is a chemokine implicated in lymphatic transmigration.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CCL21 function, confirmed by staining in Figure 4.

claim: Selective double immunostaining for D2-40 podoplanin/CD31 and for PROX1/CD31 was the most effective strategy in discriminating lymphatic vs. venous blood vessels in dura samples.
source: To accomplish this, we tested a variety of putative lymphatic endothelial markers and found that selective double immunostaining for D2-40 podoplanin/CD31 and for PROX1/CD31 was the most effective strategy in discriminating lymphatic vs. venous blood vessels in dura samples
evidence: Based on experimental testing of multiple markers as described in the methods and shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Lymphatics sprout from transdifferentiation of venous endothelium.
source: a challenging task since lymphatics sprout from transdifferentiation of venous endothelium (Ny et al., 2005; Yaniv et al., 2006; Srinivasan et al., 2007; Aspelund et al., 2014; Lowe et al., 2015) and persistently share some endothelial markers.
evidence: Based on cited references (Ny et al., 2005; Yaniv et al., 2006; Srinivasan et al., 2007; Aspelund et al., 2014; Lowe et al., 2015) describing lymphatic development.

claim: Lymphatics persistently share some endothelial markers with venous endothelium.
source: a challenging task since lymphatics sprout from transdifferentiation of venous endothelium (Ny et al., 2005; Yaniv et al., 2006; Srinivasan et al., 2007; Aspelund et al., 2014; Lowe et al., 2015) and persistently share some endothelial markers.
evidence: This is established knowledge about lymphatic biology, supported by the cited references and the need for selective double staining in the study.

claim: A branched network of lymphatics was clearly seen within the dura mater.
source: A branched network of lymphatics was clearly seen within the dura mater.
evidence: Demonstrated by histopathological images in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: A total of 93 human dural lymphatics were identified on D2-40 podoplanin/CD31 double staining.
source: On D2-40 podoplanin/CD31 double staining, we identified a total of 93 human dural lymphatics
evidence: Based on quantitative histopathological analysis.

claim: Most human dural lymphatics were collapsed.
source: On D2-40 podoplanin/CD31 double staining, we identified a total of 93 human dural lymphatics; most were collapsed, explaining the large range of maximum transverse diameters (range = 7–842 μm, mean = 125 μm, standard deviation = 161 μm).
evidence: Based on histopathological observations and measurements.

claim: The maximum transverse diameter of human dural lymphatics ranges from 7 to 842 μm, with a mean of 125 μm and standard deviation of 161 μm.
source: On D2-40 podoplanin/CD31 double staining, we identified a total of 93 human dural lymphatics; most were collapsed, explaining the large range of maximum transverse diameters (range = 7–842 μm, mean = 125 μm, standard deviation = 161 μm).
evidence: Based on quantitative histopathological measurements.

claim: The density of dural lymphatics was higher around the venous sinuses than in more lateral areas of the dura.
source: The density of dural lymphatics was higher around the venous sinuses than in more lateral areas of the dura, and higher within the meningeal layer than the periosteal layer of the dura.
evidence: Based on histopathological observations and quantification.

claim: The density of dural lymphatics was higher within the meningeal layer than the periosteal layer of the dura.
source: The density of dural lymphatics was higher around the venous sinuses than in more lateral areas of the dura, and higher within the meningeal layer than the periosteal layer of the dura.
evidence: Based on histopathological observations and quantification.

claim: At least some lymphatics are contained entirely within the dura.
source: In the ongoing debate about the precise localization of lymphatics within the meninges (either completely within the dura or 'shared' between the dura and the arachnoid) (Kipnis, 2016; Raper et al., 2016), our pathological data clearly show that at least some lymphatics are contained entirely within the dura (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by histopathological images in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The authors were unable to visualize lymphatics within the leptomeninges on limited evaluation.
source: On limited evaluation, we were unable to visualize lymphatics within the leptomeninges, but additional dedicated studies, ideally with nonconventional tissue-preparation methods, are warranted to fully explore this possibility.
evidence: Based on the authors' histopathological examination.

claim: A comprehensive map of the meningeal lymphatic network would have implications for unraveling the ways in which the meningeal lymphatics participate in waste clearance.
source: A comprehensive map of the meningeal lymphatic network would have implications for unraveling the ways in which the meningeal lymphatics participate in waste clearance and in immune cell trafficking within the central nervous system (Louveau et al., 2015a; Kipnis, 2016; Raper et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research implications, supported by cited references.

claim: A comprehensive map of the meningeal lymphatic network would have implications for unraveling the ways in which the meningeal lymphatics participate in immune cell trafficking within the central nervous system.
source: A comprehensive map of the meningeal lymphatic network would have implications for unraveling the ways in which the meningeal lymphatics participate in waste clearance and in immune cell trafficking within the central nervous system (Louveau et al., 2015a; Kipnis, 2016; Raper et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research implications, supported by cited references.

claim: In inflammatory pathological conditions, cellular migration toward the dural lymphatics might be profoundly enhanced by specific signaling and lymphatic plasticity.
source: In inflammatory pathological conditions, cellular migration toward the dural lymphatics might be profoundly enhanced by specific signaling and lymphatic plasticity (Alitalo et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2012; Stacker et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on cited references (Alitalo et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2012; Stacker et al., 2014) about lymphatic biology in inflammation.

claim: Clusters of extravascular CD3+ lymphocytes were observed in the dura of several multiple sclerosis autopsies.
source: Noteworthy in this context are clusters of extravascular CD3+ lymphocytes and CD68+ phagocytic meningeal macrophages that we observed in the dura of several multiple sclerosis autopsies (not shown), confirming intense immune cell trafficking and communication.
evidence: Based on histopathological observations in multiple sclerosis autopsy samples.

claim: Clusters of CD68+ phagocytic meningeal macrophages were observed in the dura of several multiple sclerosis autopsies.
source: Noteworthy in this context are clusters of extravascular CD3+ lymphocytes and CD68+ phagocytic meningeal macrophages that we observed in the dura of several multiple sclerosis autopsies (not shown), confirming intense immune cell trafficking and communication.
evidence: Based on histopathological observations in multiple sclerosis autopsy samples.

claim: The extensive presence of small lymphatics observed in multiple sclerosis dura samples might be the result of inflammation-mediated lymphoangiogenesis.
source: Indeed, without proper normative comparison, we cannot rule out that the extensive presence of small lymphatics observed in multiple sclerosis dura samples is the result of inflammation-mediated lymphoangiogenesis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging a limitation of the study.

claim: Lymphatic dysfunction might impair waste clearance in neurodegenerative diseases and aging.
source: On the other hand, lymphatic dysfunction might impair waste clearance in neurodegenerative diseases and aging, in line with the recently captured deposition of β-amyloid in human dura in elderly people (Kovacs et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on cited reference (Kovacs et al., 2016) about β-amyloid deposition.

claim: β-amyloid deposition has been captured in human dura in elderly people.
source: On the other hand, lymphatic dysfunction might impair waste clearance in neurodegenerative diseases and aging, in line with the recently captured deposition of β-amyloid in human dura in elderly people (Kovacs et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on cited reference (Kovacs et al., 2016).

claim: The study could not prove whether dural lymphatic vessels drain immune cells, CSF, or other substances from the brain to deep cervical lymph nodes.
source: Differently from experiments implementing injections of tracers within brain structures, here we aimed primarily to image dural lymphatic vessels in human and nonhuman primates, but we could not prove whether dural lymphatic vessels drain immune cells, CSF, or other substances from the brain to deep cervical lymph nodes
evidence: This is an explicit acknowledgment of a study limitation.

claim: The study could not assess any link between dural lymphatics and the glymphatic system.
source: Differently from experiments implementing injections of tracers within brain structures, here we aimed primarily to image dural lymphatic vessels in human and nonhuman primates, but we could not prove whether dural lymphatic vessels drain immune cells, CSF, or other substances from the brain to deep cervical lymph nodes, nor could we assess any link with the glymphatic system (Iliff et al., 2012; Xie et al., 2013; Iliff et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an explicit acknowledgment of a study limitation, with references to the glymphatic system literature.

claim: The data clearly and consistently demonstrate the existence of lymphatic vessels within the dura mater of human and nonhuman primates.
source: Overall, our data clearly and consistently demonstrate the existence of lymphatic vessels within the dura mater of human and nonhuman primates.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by all the MRI and histopathological data presented in the study.

claim: The meningeal lymphatic system is evolutionarily conserved in mammals.
source: Together with recent studies in rodents, our results show that the meningeal lymphatic system is evolutionarily conserved in mammals
evidence: This is an inference based on the current study's findings in primates and cited rodent studies (Aspelund et al., 2015; Louveau et al., 2015b).

claim: Paolo Mascagni speculated that there were lymphatic vessels at the surface of human brain exactly two centuries before this study.
source: Together with recent studies in rodents, our results show that the meningeal lymphatic system is evolutionarily conserved in mammals and confirm, after exactly two centuries, what the Italian anatomist Paolo Mascagni speculated were lymphatic vessels at the surface of human brain (Mascagni and Bellini, 1816).
evidence: Based on historical citation (Mascagni and Bellini, 1816).

claim: The ability to image the meningeal lymphatics noninvasively suggests the possibility of studying potential abnormalities in human neurological disorders.
source: The ability to image the meningeal lymphatics noninvasively immediately suggests the possibility of studying potential abnormalities in human neurological disorders.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research implications based on the demonstrated imaging capability.

claim: Human studies were carried out under a protocol (NCT02504840) approved by NIH Institutional Review Board.
source: We carried out human studies under a protocol (NCT02504840) approved by NIH Institutional Review Board.
evidence: This is a statement of regulatory compliance.

claim: Informed consent was obtained from all human participants.
source: Informed consent was obtained from all participants.
evidence: This is a statement of ethical compliance.

claim: Animal studies were performed under a protocol approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
source: Animal studies were performed under a protocol approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
evidence: This is a statement of regulatory compliance.

claim: Five healthy volunteers (three women, age range 28–53 years) were studied.
source: We studied five healthy volunteers (three women, age range 28–53 years)
evidence: This describes the human study population.

claim: Human scans were obtained on a 3-tesla MRI unit (Skyra, Siemens Healthcare).
source: We studied five healthy volunteers (three women, age range 28–53 years) and obtained scans on a 3-tesla MRI unit (Skyra, Siemens Healthcare, Erlangen, Germany), using the body coil for radiofrequency transmission and a 32-element phased array coil for reception.
evidence: This describes the imaging equipment used.

claim: Three healthy adult common marmosets (one female, two males, age range 4–11 years) were studied.
source: We studied three healthy adult common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus) (one female, two males, age range 4–11 years).
evidence: This describes the nonhuman primate study population.

claim: Experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) was induced in 2 marmosets with 0.2 mg of fresh-frozen human white matter homogenate.
source: After the baseline MRI, experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) was induced in 2 marmosets with 0.2 mg of fresh-frozen human white matter homogenate as previously described (Gaitán et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure, with citation to the method (Gaitán et al., 2014).

claim: Marmoset scans were obtained on a 7-tesla MRI unit (Avance AVIII, Bruker BioSpin).
source: Marmosets were placed in a sphinx position within the magnet, and scans were obtained on a 7-tesla MRI unit (Avance AVIII, Bruker BioSpin, Billerica, MA, USA).
evidence: This describes the imaging equipment used for marmosets.

claim: Multiple human dura samples were obtained from 2 formalin-fixed brains with longstanding progressive multiple sclerosis and from a 33-year-old with refractory epilepsy undergoing anterior temporal lobectomy.
source: Multiple human dura samples were obtained from 2 formalin-fixed brains (60- and 77-year-olds with longstanding progressive multiple sclerosis) and from a 33-year-old with refractory epilepsy undergoing anterior temporal lobectomy (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This describes the human tissue samples used for histopathology.

claim: Primate samples were obtained from 3 adult common marmosets (2 with EAE).
source: Primate samples were obtained from 3 adult common marmosets (2 with EAE) [Figure 4—source data 1].
evidence: This describes the nonhuman primate tissue samples used for histopathology.

claim: MRI-matched histological sections were achieved via 7T MRI of the fixed brain and subsequent gross sectioning with an individualized, MRI-designed, 3D-printed cutting box.
source: For primate brains, MRI-matched histological sections were achieved via 7T MRI of the fixed brain and subsequent gross sectioning with an individualized, MRI-designed, 3D-printed cutting box, as previously described (Absinta et al., 2014; Guy et al., 2016; Luciano et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the method for MRI-histopathology correlation, with citations to previous methodological papers.

claim: On conventional post-gadobutrol T1-weighted MRI, conventional imaging is unable to discriminate lymphatic vessels due to diffuse physiological enhancement of the dura and blood vessels.
source: In both species, conventional post-gadobutrol coronal T1-weighted MRI is unable to discriminate lymphatic vessels due to diffuse physiological enhancement of the dura (arrows) and blood vessels, including the superior sagittal sinus and straight sinus (arrows).
evidence: Demonstrated by MRI images in Figure 1.

claim: On post-gadobutrol T2-FLAIR, the dura does not enhance.
source: On post-gadobutrol coronal T2-FLAIR and subtraction images, the dura does not enhance, and lymphatic vessels (red arrows), running alongside the venous dural sinuses and within the falx cerebri, can be appreciated.
evidence: Demonstrated by MRI images in Figure 1.

claim: On post-gadobutrol T2-FLAIR, lymphatic vessels running alongside the venous dural sinuses and within the falx cerebri can be appreciated.
source: On post-gadobutrol coronal T2-FLAIR and subtraction images, the dura does not enhance, and lymphatic vessels (red arrows), running alongside the venous dural sinuses and within the falx cerebri, can be appreciated.
evidence: Demonstrated by MRI images in Figure 1.

claim: The choroid plexus enhanced less with gadofosveset than gadobutrol.
source: Notably, the choroid plexus (white arrows) enhanced less with gadofosveset than gadobutrol
evidence: Demonstrated by MRI images in Figure 2.

claim: Meningeal and parenchymal blood vessels (both veins and arteries) did not enhance with any contrast agent and appeared black on black-blood imaging.
source: Notably, the choroid plexus (white arrows) enhanced less with gadofosveset than gadobutrol, whereas meningeal and parenchymal blood vessels (both veins and arteries) did not enhance with any contrast agent and appeared black.
evidence: Demonstrated by MRI images in Figure 2.

claim: On conventional T1-weighted MPRAGE images, meningeal and parenchymal blood vessels enhanced with both contrast agents, more clearly with gadofosveset.
source: On conventional T1-weighted MPRAGE images, meningeal and parenchymal blood vessels enhanced with both contrast agents, more clearly with gadofosveset.
evidence: Demonstrated by MRI images in Figure 2.
